title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false-positive failure in an automated license-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a system alert is passed to a patrol deputy for enforcement. The system misread one character on a plate and produced a match to a stolen vehicle of similar description. The enforcement action, a detention at gunpoint, followed from that alert rather than from independent observation.

The failure mode is an automated identification treated as sufficient grounds for a stop, without a human check of the alert before force was used. Flock's stated position is that alerts should be independently verified before enforcement, which means the check was expected and was not performed in this case. Catching the error would have required a person to compare the alert against the actual plate, or a policy that no enforcement action follows an unverified alert. The sheriff's office attributes the misread to an illegal tinted plate cover, which is a claim about cause rather than a finding.

It is not established that the plate cover caused the misidentification, that the deputy's conduct was reasonable, or that the motorist had any connection to the stolen vehicle. The sheriff's statement and Flock's guidance are positions taken after the incident, not adjudicated conclusions.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, a 42-year-old motorist in York County, South Carolina, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety automated license-plate reader misidentified the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
